from manim import *
import numpy as np

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Fetching storyboard data
        title_text = "Introduction: The Hidden Pattern"
        lecture_lines = [
            "Some data distributions look messy and chaotic.",
            "This randomness creates a sense of total chaos.",
            "A hidden order emerges when we group data.",
            "The peak represents the most common sample mean.",
            "This phenomenon is the Central Limit Theorem."
        ]
        
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)
        
        # Colors for matching animation elements
        COLOR_HIST = "#FF0000"
        COLOR_CHAOS = "#FFFFFF"
        COLOR_CURVE = "#0000FF"
        COLOR_PEAK = "#FFFF00"
        COLOR_CLT = "#FFFFFF"
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(COLOR_HIST))
        
        # Create a chaotic, bimodal histogram
        bar_heights = [1.2, 2.5, 1.0, 0.4, 0.6, 2.2, 2.8, 1.4]
        histogram = VGroup(*[
            Rectangle(
                width=0.4, 
                height=h, 
                fill_opacity=0.8, 
                fill_color=COLOR_HIST, 
                stroke_color=WHITE, 
                stroke_width=1
            )
            for h in bar_heights
        ]).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0.1, aligned_edge=DOWN)
        
        self.place_in_area(histogram, "B1", "E6")
        self.play(Create(histogram))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(COLOR_CHAOS)
        )
        
        chaos_text = Text("CHAOS", font_size=36, weight=BOLD, color=COLOR_CHAOS)
        # Position chaos_text above the histogram
        self.place_in_area(chaos_text, "A1", "A6")
        
        self.play(Write(chaos_text))
        self.play(Indicate(chaos_text, color=COLOR_HIST))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(COLOR_CURVE)
        )
        
        # Create a smooth blue Bell Curve (Normal Distribution approximation)
        axes = Axes(
            x_range=[-3, 3], y_range=[0, 1],
            x_length=5, y_length=3,
            axis_config={"include_tip": False}
        )
        
        curve = axes.plot(lambda x: np.exp(-x**2), color=COLOR_CURVE, x_range=[-2.5, 2.5])
        curve_group = VGroup(curve)
        self.place_in_area(curve_group, "B1", "E6")
        
        self.play(
            FadeOut(chaos_text),
            ReplacementTransform(histogram, curve_group)
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(COLOR_PEAK)
        )
        
        # Highlight the peak of the Bell Curve with a yellow vertical line
        peak_top = curve_group.get_top()
        # The bottom of the curve is determined by its lowest points
        peak_bottom = np.array([peak_top[0], curve_group.get_bottom()[1], 0])
        peak_line = Line(
            start=peak_top,
            end=peak_bottom,
            color=COLOR_PEAK,
            stroke_width=5
        )
        
        self.play(Create(peak_line))
        self.play(Flash(peak_line, color=COLOR_PEAK))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.play(
            self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(WHITE),
            self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(COLOR_CLT)
        )
        
        clt_text = Text("Central Limit Theorem", font_size=32, color=COLOR_CLT)
        # Position CLT text below the curve
        self.place_in_area(clt_text, "F1", "F6")
        
        self.play(FadeIn(clt_text))
        self.wait(2)
        
        # Reset color and finish
        self.play(self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        self.wait(2)

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Title and Lecture Lines
        title_text = "Prerequisite Checklist: Population vs. Sample"
        lecture_lines = [
            "The population includes every individual in a group.",
            "We select a sample to measure and label.",
            "Scaling up the sample allows for detailed analysis."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)

        # Colors
        pop_color = "#FFFFFF"
        sample_color = "#00FF00"

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Display a large cloud of small white (#FFFFFF) dots representing the population.
        self.lecture[0].set_color(YELLOW)
        
        # Population cloud
        np.random.seed(42)
        pop_dots = VGroup(*[Dot(radius=0.04, color=pop_color) for _ in range(120)])
        
        # Scatter them in area B2 to E5
        for dot in pop_dots:
            dot.move_to(np.array([
                np.random.uniform(1.0, 5.0),
                np.random.uniform(-2.2, 1.8),
                0
            ]))
            
        # Using Text instead of MathTex to avoid LaTeX dependency error
        pop_label = Text("Population (μ)", color=pop_color)
        self.place_at_grid(pop_label, "A3", scale_factor=0.6)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(pop_dots), Write(pop_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Draw a green (#00FF00) circle around a group of dots and label them 'Population (μ)' and 'Sample (x̄)'.
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color(YELLOW)

        # Sample selection
        sample_center = self.grid["D4"]
        sample_circle = Circle(radius=0.8, color=sample_color, stroke_width=4)
        sample_circle.move_to(sample_center)
        
        # Using Text instead of MathTex to avoid LaTeX dependency error
        sample_label = Text("Sample (x̄)", color=sample_color)
        self.place_at_grid(sample_label, "F4", scale_factor=0.6)

        # Distinguish dots: some dots turn green to indicate they are in the sample
        dots_inside = VGroup()
        dots_outside = VGroup()
        for dot in pop_dots:
            if np.linalg.norm(dot.get_center() - sample_center) < 0.8:
                dot.set_color(sample_color)
                dots_inside.add(dot)
            else:
                dots_outside.add(dot)
        
        # Ensure enough dots are inside for visual clarity
        if len(dots_inside) < 10:
            for _ in range(10 - len(dots_inside)):
                offset = np.random.uniform(-0.6, 0.6, size=3)
                offset[2] = 0
                d = Dot(radius=0.04, color=sample_color).move_to(sample_center + offset)
                dots_inside.add(d)
                pop_dots.add(d)

        self.play(Create(sample_circle))
        self.play(Write(sample_label))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Scale up the green circle until it fills the screen, showing the sampled dots clearly.
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color(YELLOW)

        # Scaling and focus
        target_pos = self.grid["C3"]
        
        # We group sample elements to scale together
        sample_view = VGroup(sample_circle, dots_inside, sample_label)
        
        # We fade out everything else to focus on the sample
        self.play(
            FadeOut(dots_outside),
            FadeOut(pop_label),
            sample_view.animate.scale(2.5).move_to(target_pos),
            run_time=2
        )
        self.wait(2)
        
        # Final state
        self.lecture[2].set_color(WHITE)
        self.wait(1)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Setup data from storyboard
        title_text = "The Experiment: Sampling the Squirrels"
        lecture_lines = [
            "We calculate the average weight of squirrel groups.",
            "Each sample mean becomes a single data point.",
            "Repeating this process creates a new data distribution."
        ]
        self.setup_layout(title_text, lecture_lines)

        # Colors from storyboard
        GREY_COLOR = "#808080"
        BLUE_COLOR = "#0000FF"
        
        # Static elements: Axis at the bottom (Row F)
        axis = Line(self.grid["F1"], self.grid["F6"], color=WHITE)
        axis_label = Text("Sample Mean Weight", font_size=16, color=WHITE).next_to(axis, DOWN, buff=0.2)
        self.add(axis, axis_label)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Color line 1 to match elements (Grey)
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(GREY_COLOR))
        
        # 10 grey squares representing individual squirrels
        squirrels = VGroup(*[Square(side_length=0.2, color=GREY_COLOR, fill_opacity=0.8) for _ in range(10)])
        squirrels.arrange_in_grid(rows=2, cols=5, buff=0.1)
        self.place_in_area(squirrels, "B2", "C5")
        
        self.play(FadeIn(squirrels))
        self.wait(0.5)
        
        # Calculate average and display number above a blue dot
        avg_val = 502
        avg_label = Text(f"{avg_val}g", font_size=20, color=WHITE)
        sample_dot = Dot(color=BLUE_COLOR, radius=0.1)
        self.place_at_grid(sample_dot, "D3")
        avg_label.next_to(sample_dot, UP, buff=0.1)
        
        self.play(
            Write(avg_label),
            FadeIn(sample_dot)
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Color line 2 to match elements (Blue)
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(BLUE_COLOR))
        
        # The blue dot falls vertically onto the axis
        # Vertical fall from D3 to F3
        target_x = self.grid["D3"][0]
        target_y = self.grid["F3"][1] + 0.1
        
        self.play(
            sample_dot.animate.move_to([target_x, target_y, 0]),
            FadeOut(avg_label),
            FadeOut(squirrels),
            run_time=1.5
        )
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Color line 3 to match elements (Blue)
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(BLUE_COLOR))
        
        # Stacking logic setup
        bin_counts = {}
        bin_width = 0.3
        
        def get_stack_pos(x_val):
            # Map x_val to a bin index based on the axis range
            bin_idx = int((x_val - self.grid["F1"][0]) / bin_width)
            count = bin_counts.get(bin_idx, 0)
            bin_counts[bin_idx] = count + 1
            # Stack dots upwards from the axis
            return np.array([self.grid["F1"][0] + bin_idx * bin_width + bin_width/2, self.grid["F1"][1] + 0.1 + count * 0.12, 0])

        # Register the first dot in the bins
        first_bin_idx = int((target_x - self.grid["F1"][0]) / bin_width)
        bin_counts[first_bin_idx] = 1

        # Repeat the process 5 times
        for _ in range(5):
            # Flash squirrel group
            temp_sq = VGroup(*[Square(side_length=0.12, color=GREY_COLOR, fill_opacity=0.6) for _ in range(10)])
            temp_sq.arrange_in_grid(rows=2, cols=5, buff=0.05)
            self.place_in_area(temp_sq, "B2", "C5")
            
            # Generate a new sample mean dot
            rand_x = self.grid["D3"][0] + random.uniform(-1.5, 1.5)
            new_dot = Dot(color=BLUE_COLOR, radius=0.08)
            new_dot.move_to([rand_x, self.grid["D3"][1], 0])
            
            self.play(
                FadeIn(temp_sq, run_time=0.2),
                FadeIn(new_dot, run_time=0.2)
            )
            
            # Dot falls and stacks
            stack_pos = get_stack_pos(rand_x)
            self.play(
                new_dot.animate.move_to(stack_pos),
                FadeOut(temp_sq, run_time=0.2),
                run_time=0.6
            )

        # Speed up the process (Continuous dots falling)
        fast_dots_animations = []
        for i in range(40):
            # Sampling from a normal-like distribution for visual effect
            rand_x = random.gauss(self.grid["D3"][0], 0.8)
            # Clamp to axis bounds
            rand_x = max(self.grid["F1"][0] + 0.2, min(self.grid["F6"][0] - 0.2, rand_x))
            
            fast_dot = Dot(color=BLUE_COLOR, radius=0.06)
            # Start falling from above (off-grid Row A)
            start_pos = np.array([rand_x, 3.5, 0])
            fast_dot.move_to(start_pos)
            
            stack_pos = get_stack_pos(rand_x)
            
            # Create a sequence: wait then move
            delay = i * 0.05
            anim = Succession(
                Wait(delay),
                fast_dot.animate.move_to(stack_pos).set_run_time(0.2)
            )
            self.add(fast_dot)
            fast_dots_animations.append(anim)

        self.play(AnimationGroup(*fast_dots_animations))
        self.wait(3)

class Section4Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        # Initialize layout
        self.setup_layout("The Convergence: The Birth of the Bell", [
            "- Watch as sample means begin to pile up.",
            "- A symmetric bell shape naturally starts to form.",
            "- This is the birth of the Normal Distribution."
        ])
        
        # Define hex colors
        BLUE_HEX = "#0000FF"
        WHITE_HEX = "#FFFFFF"

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Lecture: "- Watch as sample means begin to pile up."
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(BLUE_HEX))
        
        # Create horizontal axis on grid row F
        axis = Line(self.grid["F1"], self.grid["F6"], color=WHITE)
        axis_label = Text("Sample Means", font_size=16, color=WHITE)
        # Position label near axis (within 1 grid unit)
        self.place_at_grid(axis_label, "F3", scale_factor=1.0)
        axis_label.shift(DOWN * 0.5)
        
        self.add(axis, axis_label)
        
        # Create bars to represent piling dots
        bars = VGroup()
        for i in range(1, 7):
            # Initial tiny bar
            bar = Rectangle(
                width=0.6, 
                height=0.01, 
                fill_color=BLUE_HEX, 
                fill_opacity=0.7, 
                stroke_width=1, 
                stroke_color=BLUE_HEX
            )
            # Center bar horizontally at grid column i, vertically at Row F
            self.place_at_grid(bar, f"F{i}")
            bars.add(bar)
        
        self.add(bars)
        
        # Grow bars into a jagged distribution
        rough_heights = [0.4, 2.2, 1.8, 3.1, 1.2, 0.6]
        self.play(
            *[bar.animate.stretch_to_fit_height(h, about_edge=DOWN) for bar, h in zip(bars, rough_heights)],
            run_time=2.5,
            rate_func=smooth
        )
        self.wait(0.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Lecture: "- A symmetric bell shape naturally starts to form."
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(BLUE_HEX))
        
        # Smooth into symmetric bell heights
        smooth_heights = [0.6, 2.0, 3.5, 3.5, 2.0, 0.6]
        self.play(
            *[bar.animate.stretch_to_fit_height(h, about_edge=DOWN) for bar, h in zip(bars, smooth_heights)],
            run_time=1.5
        )
        self.wait(0.5)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Lecture: "- This is the birth of the Normal Distribution."
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(WHITE_HEX))
        
        # Create the ideal Normal Distribution curve
        def normal_pdf_func(x):
            # Symmetric curve peaking at 3.5
            return 3.5 * np.exp(-0.5 * (x / 0.8)**2)
            
        curve = FunctionGraph(
            normal_pdf_func,
            x_range=[-2.5, 2.5],
            color=WHITE_HEX,
            stroke_width=4
        )
        
        # Align curve with the axis and bars
        # Grid center for Row F is between F3 and F4
        dist_center = (self.grid["F3"] + self.grid["F4"]) / 2
        curve.move_to(dist_center, aligned_edge=DOWN)
        
        # Add glow effect
        glow = curve.copy().set_stroke(width=12, opacity=0.3, color=WHITE_HEX)
        
        # Animate curve creation
        self.play(Create(curve), FadeIn(glow), run_time=2)
        
        # Flash animation to emphasize shape
        self.play(
            curve.animate.set_stroke(width=8), 
            glow.animate.set_stroke(width=20, opacity=0.5), 
            run_time=0.4
        )
        self.play(
            curve.animate.set_stroke(width=4), 
            glow.animate.set_stroke(width=12, opacity=0.3), 
            run_time=0.4
        )
        
        self.wait(2)

                "Start with any distribution, no matter how chaotic.",

                "Ensure sample size is at least thirty.",
                "The results will always follow a bell curve.",
                "Statistics transforms chaos into clear, actionable order."
            ]
        )

        # Colors for mapping lines to animations
        COLOR_CHAOS = "#FF5555"
        COLOR_BRIDGE = "#FFFFFF"
        COLOR_STEPS = "#55AAFF"
        COLOR_NORMAL = "#FFD700"
        COLOR_ORDER = "#00FFFF"

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # "Start with any distribution, no matter how chaotic."
        self.lecture[0].set_color(COLOR_CHAOS)
        
        # Chaos Group: Random primitive shapes
        chaos_elements = VGroup()
        for _ in range(15):
            # Using random.choice instead of np.random.choice to avoid array dimension issues with Mobjects
            shape = random.choice([
                Circle(radius=0.1, color=COLOR_CHAOS, fill_opacity=0.6),
                Square(side_length=0.2, color=COLOR_CHAOS, fill_opacity=0.6),
                Triangle(color=COLOR_CHAOS, fill_opacity=0.6).scale(0.12)
            ])
            # Spread shapes around a relative center
            shape.shift(np.random.uniform(-0.7, 0.7, 3))
            chaos_elements.add(shape)
        
        self.place_in_area(chaos_elements, "B1", "D2", scale_factor=1.0)
        
        # Faint bell curve on the right representing the goal
        axes = Axes(
            x_range=[-3, 3], y_range=[0, 0.5], 
            axis_config={"include_tip": False, "stroke_width": 1},
            tips=False
        ).set_color(GRAY)
        bell_curve_plot = axes.plot(lambda x: 0.4 * np.exp(-x**2 / 2), color=COLOR_NORMAL, stroke_opacity=0.3)
        bell_group = VGroup(axes, bell_curve_plot)

        self.play(Create(chaos_elements), FadeIn(bell_group))
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===

        self.lecture[1].set_color(COLOR_BRIDGE)

outline.topic: The Magic of the Central Limit Theorem: Order from Chaos
outline.target_audience: Introductory Statistics Students / Undergraduate University Students

sections.title: Introduction: The Hidden Pattern
sections.content: Start with a visual of a chaotic, 'ugly' distribution (e.g., a bimodal or skewed histogram). Introduce the mystery: no matter how weird the starting population looks, if we group them together, a perfect 'Bell Curve' emerges. Explain that this is the Central Limit Theorem (CLT).
sections.example: Imagine a forest where animal weights are completely random—some tiny beetles, some massive elephants, and nothing in between. The graph looks like a mess.

sections.title: Prerequisite Checklist: Population vs. Sample
sections.content: Briefly define the 'Population' (everyone) and its Mean (μ). Contrast this with a 'Sample' (a small group) and its Mean (x̄). Use a magnifying glass graphic to show picking a small group out of the large crowd.
sections.example: Population: All 1,000 squirrels in the park. Sample: A random group of 30 squirrels we caught and weighed today.

sections.title: The Experiment: Sampling the Squirrels
sections.content: Introduce the process of repeated sampling. We take a sample of size 'n', calculate the mean, and plot it on a new graph. Then we do it again. And again. Visualize a 'Mean-o-Matic' machine that takes groups of squirrels and spits out a single average weight dot.
sections.example: Robot 'Sample-Bot' picks 10 random squirrels, averages their weight to 500g, and drops a blue marble on a scale. It repeats this 1,000 times.

sections.title: The Convergence: The Birth of the Bell
sections.content: Show an animation where the 'Sample Means' histogram starts to pile up. Even if the original squirrel weights were skewed, the pile of blue marbles starts to form a symmetric Normal Distribution shape. Highlight the key concept: The distribution of sample means is always Normal if the sample size is large enough.
sections.example: As 'n' (the number of squirrels in each group) increases from 2 to 30, the jagged graph of dots magically smooths out into a perfect, glowing Bell Curve.

sections.title: The Golden Rule: Sample Size (n ≥ 30)
sections.content: Introduce the mathematical 'Magic Number' 30. Explain that for most distributions, once your sample size reaches 30, the CLT 'kicks in' and the normal approximation becomes reliable. Use a 'Power Meter' visual that turns green when n reaches 30.
sections.example: If 'Sample-Bot' only picks 2 squirrels, the graph is still messy. When it picks 30 squirrels per group, the Bell Curve becomes undeniable.

sections.title: The Math: Mean and Standard Error
sections.content: Introduce the formulas graphically. The center of the new Bell Curve is the same as the original population mean (μ). However, the Bell Curve is narrower. Show the formula for Standard Error: σ / √n. Visually demonstrate that as 'n' gets bigger, the Bell Curve gets taller and skinnier (more precise).
sections.example: Show a wide, flat bell curve for n=30 and a very thin, sharp needle-like bell curve for n=1000, representing higher certainty.

sections.title: Real-World Application: Quality Control
sections.content: Explain why this matters. Since we know the shape of sample means is a Bell Curve, we can predict probabilities even if we don't know the full population distribution. This is used in everything from medical trials to manufacturing.
sections.example: A candy factory bot measures the average sugar in 50 bars. Even if some bars are slightly off, CLT tells the manager the probability that the *average* of the batch is within safety limits.

sections.title: Summary: The Bridge to Statistics
sections.content: Recap: 1. Start with any distribution. 2. Take large samples (n ≥ 30). 3. The means will be Normally distributed. Conclude that the CLT is the bridge that allows us to use Normal Distribution math on almost anything in the universe.
sections.example: Final visual: A bridge made of Bell Curves connecting a chaotic world of data to a structured world of scientific prediction.

storyboard.title: Introduction: The Hidden Pattern
lecture_lines: Some data distributions look messy and chaotic.
This randomness creates a sense of total chaos.
A hidden order emerges when we group data.
The peak represents the most common sample mean.
This phenomenon is the Central Limit Theorem.

Fade in the text 'Central Limit Theorem' in white (#FFFFFF) below the curve.

Draw a green (#00FF00) circle around a group of dots [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/dots.svg] and label them 'Population (μ)' and 'Sample (x̄)'.
Scale up the green circle until it fills the screen, showing the sampled dots [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/dots.svg] clearly.

storyboard.title: The Experiment: Sampling the Squirrels
lecture_lines: We calculate the average weight of squirrel groups.
Each sample mean becomes a single data point.
Repeating this process creates a new data distribution.
animations: Show a group of 10 squirrels [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/squirrel.svg] and display their average weight above them.
Move the average value down to a horizontal axis as a blue (#0000FF) dot.
Rapidly stack hundreds of blue (#0000FF) dots on the axis to show a distribution forming.

storyboard.title: The Convergence: The Birth of the Bell
lecture_lines: Watch as sample means begin to pile up.
A symmetric bell shape naturally starts to form.
This is the birth of the Normal Distribution.
animations: Transform the pile of blue (#0000FF) dots into a jagged vertical bar histogram.
Smooth the jagged bars into a solid blue (#0000FF) bell-shaped area.
Overlay a glowing white (#FFFFFF) Normal Distribution curve with a pulse effect.

storyboard.title: The Golden Rule: Sample Size (n ≥ 30)
lecture_lines: Small samples often result in messy distributions.
Increasing the sample size fills the power meter.
Reliability is reached once n reaches thirty.
animations: Display a jagged red (#FF0000) histogram labeled 'n = 2' with a low red power meter [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/meter.svg].
Animate the power meter [Asset: /mmfs1/data/group/pmc082/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/meter.svg] filling to green (#00FF00) as the label changes to 'n = 30'.
Transform the red histogram into a smooth green (#00FF00) Bell Curve.

storyboard.title: The Math: Mean and Standard Error
lecture_lines: The curve stays centered on the population mean.
We calculate variation using the Standard Error formula.
Small samples produce a wider, flatter bell curve.
Larger samples provide much higher statistical certainty.
Precision increases with the square root of n.
animations: Display the formula 'μ_x̄ = μ' in white (#FFFFFF) at the top of the screen.
Display 'Standard Error: σ_x̄ = σ / √n' below it in white.
Show a wide, flat Bell Curve in blue (#0000FF) representing n=30.
Animate the curve becoming taller and narrower as 'n' increases to 1000.
Highlight the '√n' in the formula with yellow (#FFFF00) as the curve narrows.

storyboard.title: Real-World Application: Quality Control
lecture_lines: We monitor candy bars on a factory line.
Sample means must fall within safe bell limits.
This guarantees consistent quality for every batch.
animations: Show orange (#FFA500) candy bars moving past a blue (#0000FF) scanning line.
Drop a blue (#0000FF) dot into the green (#00FF00) safe region of a Bell Curve.
Fade in 'Quality Guaranteed' in green (#00FF00) with a subtle glow.

storyboard.title: Summary: The Bridge to Statistics
lecture_lines: Start with any distribution, no matter how chaotic.
Build a bridge toward structured scientific prediction.
Ensure sample size is at least thirty.
The results will always follow a bell curve.
Statistics transforms chaos into clear, actionable order.
animations: Show a chaotic mix of shapes on the left and a Bell Curve on the right.
Draw a solid white (#FFFFFF) bridge connecting the two sides.
Display the steps '1. Any Data', '2. n ≥ 30', '3. Normal Shape' along the bridge.
The entire scene glows as the text 'Order from Chaos' appears above.
The bridge and labels fade out, leaving a single golden (#FFD700) Bell Curve.
